title: I'm going to beach
html:
Part 1

Imagine I found a glitch in the matrix -- or to simplify -- I found $100M that just appeared in my bank account one fine day. What's stopping me from running to the beach and leaving everything  behind that I call dear? Once I find that money, will I think about my dream of making AI more interpretable and safe? For more than just a moment, I will seriously consider flying to the Caribbean islands, get a nice yacht, and have fun. I will also very likely go ahead and do it -- even if it is just for some time. 

Humans are indeed optimized for reproductive success. 

This optimization has happened through pleasure-like proxies. Now that we're in a world where pleasure is accessible at the click of a button, we just can't stop ourselves from pressing it forever.  For e.g. I know I'm not supposed to wake up and open Twitter first thing and yet here we are. 

Am I misaligned? 

I wouldn't blame myself for splurging those $100,000,000. I would definitely blame myself if I didn't splurge. I don't think I'm misaligned because I think this. It actually makes complete sense from the inside. 

Will I actively go out and try to find a glitch that deposits $100M in my account, though? I wouldn't even dare. Probably because it's illegal. I won't do it, but not because it's unethical. I know the law says that it's a crime, it's against the spirit of the society, and all that. We're also not in a race against each other to find the glitch first. Most of us know the systems are secure enough and we're not capable of doing it. We know we're not capable. So much so that we'd not even try. 

[Alright, so let's all try and all get rich!!!]

If no one played by the rules, will we even be on a planet we like to call home? A huge part of the appeal of staying here is that our constraints are physical, social, legal, and also ethical, as a cherry on the top. The world is fun because of these constraints, not in spite of them! 

But, man, do I want to go to the beach. 

To me, when we talk about alignment (or intent-alignment in particular), it means our AI not wanting to go to the beach. Inspired by Paul Christiano's intent-alignment: we want our AI to do what H would want it to do.

We'd want our agent to not try to rob the bank, or try to create money magically. We'd want the agent to understand that we just want it to work on technical AI safety. 

Hedonic adaptation will make me want to get back to work pretty quickly. I'll still want to go and make AI safer, and make sure people actually benefit from it, and make sure it doesn't kill anyone. The beach can keep me entertained only for so long.

The reward is not the optimization target, after all [TurnTrout]. We love the delta. We like knowing the difference between where we are and where we want to get to. We're optimized to reduce that gap. We're mesa-optimizers in that sense. 

Who is to say that AGI will not rob the bank and go to the beach? If I, as a human, can presage that the beach is not that important, superintelligence will probably be at least a few steps ahead of that. 

But then, I actually don't worry about AGI going to the beach. I worry that the AGI will, in fact, not go. AGI could very well be a mesa-optimizer, and could let us go extinct. It'll be a master at realizing that the beach is not the point, and will be hyper-focused on an abstract goal that it has learned.

[And hence we arrive at the squiggle-paperclip-maximizer from first principles; I can at least imitate arriving here and it doesn't feel contrived.] 

I acknowledge that a lot of this has been already said. It's still important to face the stakes myself. I am personally incapable of imagining what AGI will look like. I don't think anyone is. But just this simple chain-of-thought paints a pretty grim picture. 

Then why are we trying to build better AIs? 

As humans, we want to live. 

I, personally, want to see a cure for cancer (and all bad diseases) and see poverty eradicated. I want all humans to be happy. And I want it now. I think all humans would like to see these problems solved. 

Superintelligence brings the promise of solving everything, in our own lifetimes. I cannot ignore the fact that I'm writing this on a day when Riemann Hypothesis is claimed to have been proven. Things we would only call miracles are happening. Isn't it all exciting? And we're not even close to AGI right now. We're far away from the mesa-optimizing monster that I feared, right? 

Why not just push this technology until we solve these 3 problems and then stop? 

Can we, though? 

Can we precisely figure out which problems we want to solve, and stop right there? Say cancer was solved today. It's done. No back-propagation allowed on any GPUs starting right now. 

I lost a cousin to cancer, and every reader, I'm sure, has had their personal experience. I am totally in support of no one dying of cancer. But when have we, as humans, ever stopped? We seem to be in an unstoppable march. Don't know towards what. Just, more? 

First, we wanted to control fire because we just wanted good food, better security. Would you go back in time and stop the stone age humans from controlling fire because we didn't stop just there? 

"They just say they want better nutrition and security right now, but actually they're going to end up inventing agriculture, then form cities, then printing press, then science, then the computer, and then... you know. Where does this go from here? We cannot let this happen. We don't trust these people to take the best steps."

Controlling fire was actually a good step our ancestors took. I think it is unfair to say that we will solve only these three problems and then stop. We won't. We won't make our AI just more capable until we solve X. 

We won't, by definition stop at just cancer. With all our faults, we still march on. Our history is full of atrocities and violence, no doubt, but do we think we did a bad thing by controlling fire? I wouldn't say so. 

Every new technology comes in and promises something revolutionary. Electricity brought its own revolution, the printing press did before it, and computers did after. Each technology ushered us into a new era in their own way. 

Ha. 

Fire didn't act on its own. We did. We shaped everything that followed fire. 

The printing press didn't print without a human writing something up. The science experiments didn't conduct themselves. The steam engine didn't produce factories on its own. 

GPT-6.2-Astra, on the other hand, solved* the Navier-Stokes Millennium prize problem. These models, which we see just about 6 years into the age of LLMs, have made a dent (more than a dent, to be fair) in fields where only humans thought they had primacy. 

Fire never threatened to solve everything for us. AI does. None of the tools before ever did. This tool will take control. We will happily submit to the tool because it promises us things we think we want. 

A sufficiently intelligent AI model acts on its own now. And it will do so increasingly. Even if agents are "tied" to humans, a large portion of what they do risks remaining obscure and unknown to humans. This is cruelly illustrated by how Claude produced a proof for RH not a lot of humans have come close to understanding right when this happened. I don't think this is a one-off event.
